Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette:
Leila was 68 when she finally agreed to start talking about what had changed in her life since the assault at work, though even then she spoke of it in fragments, circling the facts as if naming them too directly might summon the same danger back into the room. She had worked for years as a prison guard, a job she took seriously and knew how to do, moving through the noise and routines of the facility with a practiced vigilance. The assault happened during a shift that had seemed ordinary at first and then suddenly did not feel ordinary at all: a confrontation in the prison environment that turned physical before she could fully register what was happening. What stayed with her was not only the force of the attack but the speed of it, the way her body had already jolted into readiness before her mind had caught up. Even now, she described how she felt herself react first, her muscles tightening and her chest narrowing before she had formed any clear thought, as though danger announced itself in her body before she had time to name it.

In the months after the assault, Leila found herself living in a state of watchfulness that had become ordinary to her. She said she was constantly scanning rooms, hallways, and public spaces for signs that something was wrong, her eyes moving automatically toward doors, exits, and the people around her. At the prison, that meant standing with her attention split between the task in front of her and every small change in movement or tone around her. Off duty, it followed her into grocery stores, parking lots, and family gatherings, where she would still position herself where she could see who was coming and going. She had come to rely on staying surrounded by people, arranging visits, errands, and calls so that she would not have to be alone with her thoughts. Silence bothered her in a particular way; an unusual quiet in the house or a lull in conversation could make her feel that something dangerous was about to happen. She would look up sharply at stillness, listening for what was missing, her whole body tense before any clear reason arrived.

Sleep became difficult as those weeks turned into months. Leila lay awake longer than she used to, and when she did sleep, she often woke during the night feeling keyed up and unable to settle again. She did not describe vivid dreams so much as a restless body that would not fully let go, as if it remained on duty even in the dark. At times, when she was trying to fall asleep, she found herself replaying the feeling of being caught off guard, though she was careful not to dwell on the details for long. Instead, she would get up, turn on a light, and move into the living room or call someone, preferring the company and noise to the stillness of bed.

Her efforts to stay safe reshaped her life in practical ways. Leila began giving up responsibilities she would once have taken on without hesitation, stepping back from duties that put her in situations she found too exposed. She became more willing to let others handle tasks she had previously managed herself, even when she felt uneasy about being seen as less dependable. That change was painful to her. She had always taken pride in being reliable, especially in a role where alertness and responsibility mattered, and she felt the loss of that identity keenly. She also struggled with the belief that she should have protected others and failed. When she spoke of the assault, there was a strong current of self-reproach in the way she described it, as though the worst part were not only what happened to her but that she had not kept others safe in the moment she believed she ought to have. Alongside that was a deeper, quieter shift in how she saw herself among other people. She said she felt permanently like an outsider now, as though the event had set her apart in a way that could not be reversed. She could still be with her family, still work, still carry on ordinary conversations, but she did so with the sense that she no longer belonged in the same uncomplicated way.

Trust became harder for her as well. Leila said plainly that people could not be trusted, and she spoke as if this were not a mood but a hard-earned conclusion. That belief showed itself in the care with which she watched others, especially in unfamiliar settings or in the prison where the original assault had occurred. It also made her lean on socialising as a shield, keeping herself busy with people so there would be no quiet moment for fear or memory to take hold. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of danger, by the disrupted sleep, and by the constant alertness that followed her everywhere. What finally brought her in was the sense that she could no longer keep living as if every silence hid a threat. She wanted some relief from the feeling that her body was always bracing for harm, and she was most afraid that if she stopped scanning, stopped staying busy, or stopped handing off responsibility, she would be caught again before she had time to think.
